records.title: Chest pain
records.summary: Chest pain or pressure, especially with sweating, breathlessness or an abnormal heart rate.

data.trigger: Chest pain or pressure, especially with sweating, breathlessness or an abnormal heart rate.
steps: Stop all activity and stabilise the crew member with restraints
Measure heart rate, blood pressure and SpO₂; attach ECG if available
Give oxygen if SpO₂ is below 94%
Aspirin to chew unless allergic or bleeding risk
Nitroglycerin under the tongue only if systolic BP is above 100
Record time of onset and every reading
data.escalate: Immediately. Notify the crew medical officer and commander, and send data to the flight surgeon at the first opportunity.
data.comms_note: On Mars, the onboard team must act for 6-44 min before the first possible ground reply.

records.title: Cardiac arrest (CPR in weightlessness)
records.summary: Unresponsive, not breathing normally, no pulse.

data.trigger: Unresponsive, not breathing normally, no pulse.
steps: Call for all crew; one person gets the defibrillator and medical kit
Restrain the patient to a rigid surface such as the CPR restraint board
Start compressions: in microgravity, use the handstand method (feet braced on the ceiling) or the Evetts-Russomano method (legs wrapped around the patient's torso)
Attach defibrillator pads and follow its prompts
Ventilate with a bag-valve mask and oxygen
data.escalate: Immediately. Commander leads; ground is informed but cannot direct in time beyond low Earth orbit.
data.comms_note: Decisions about stopping resuscitation are pre-agreed in flight rules.

records.title: Fainting or dizziness on standing
records.summary: Fainting, near-fainting or light-headedness, especially after landing or in partial gravity.

data.trigger: Fainting, near-fainting or light-headedness, especially after landing or in partial gravity.
steps: Lie the person flat with legs raised
Measure blood pressure and heart rate lying and then sitting
Give fluids with salt
Check blood sugar
Use compression garments when upright
data.escalate: Same day if it repeats or comes with chest pain or palpitations.
data.comms_note: Common after landing because the body adapted to weightlessness.

records.title: Low blood oxygen
records.summary: SpO₂ below 92% on a warm finger, confirmed on a second finger.

data.trigger: SpO₂ below 92% on a warm finger, confirmed on a second finger.
steps: Re-check on another finger and with a second oximeter
Check cabin O₂ and CO₂ readouts immediately
If more than one crew member is affected, treat it as a cabin atmosphere emergency
Give supplemental oxygen by mask
Look for breathlessness, chest pain or blue lips
data.escalate: Immediately if below 90% or with symptoms.
data.comms_note: Cabin atmosphere faults are vehicle emergencies that follow separate checklists.

records.title: High CO₂ headache
records.summary: Headache, poor concentration or breathlessness while cabin CO₂ is elevated.

data.trigger: Headache, poor concentration or breathlessness while cabin CO₂ is elevated.
steps: Check CO₂ partial pressure on the cabin display
Move to an area with better ventilation and use a fan
Report to the vehicle engineer
Pain relief if needed
Track headaches against CO₂ readings in the log
data.escalate: If symptoms persist after CO₂ is corrected.
data.comms_note: ISS CO₂ levels are well above Earth's. Air flow is critical because exhaled CO₂ can pool around the face without convection.

records.title: Fever and suspected infection
records.summary: Temperature above 38.0 °C, or above 37.5 °C with symptoms.

data.trigger: Temperature above 38.0 °C, or above 37.5 °C with symptoms.
steps: Re-measure after 30 minutes of rest
Note symptoms: sore throat, cough, rash, urinary symptoms, stiff neck
Give fluids and fever relief
Limit close contact; use masks; clean shared surfaces
Report daily temperature trends
data.escalate: Same day if above 38 °C for 24 h, or immediately with rash, stiff neck, confusion or breathing difficulty.
data.comms_note: A closed habitat spreads germs quickly; early isolation protects the whole crew.

records.title: Low blood sugar
records.summary: Blood sugar below 70 mg/dL, or shakiness, sweating or confusion.

data.trigger: Blood sugar below 70 mg/dL, or shakiness, sweating or confusion.
steps: Take 15 g of fast sugar such as glucose gel
Re-check after 15 minutes; repeat if still below 70
Once above 70, eat a snack with protein and carbohydrate
Look for the cause: missed meal, intense exercise, under-eating
data.escalate: If it does not respond to two treatments, or the person becomes confused.
data.comms_note: Under-eating is common in flight, so watch for repeat episodes.

records.title: High fasting blood sugar
records.summary: Fasting blood sugar above 125 mg/dL on more than one day.

data.trigger: Fasting blood sugar above 125 mg/dL on more than one day.
steps: Re-test the next morning, fasting
Review food, exercise and sleep
Check for infection or steroid use
Log readings for trend review
data.escalate: Next medical conference if repeated, sooner with thirst, frequent urination or confusion.
data.comms_note: Inactivity and spaceflight can reduce insulin sensitivity.

records.title: Solar particle event (storm shelter)
records.summary: Space weather alert, or dosimeter dose several times the normal rate.

data.trigger: Space weather alert, or dosimeter dose several times the normal rate.
steps: Stop or abort EVA and surface traverses
Go to the designated storm shelter: the most shielded part of the vehicle
Add mass around the crew: water bags, food, supplies
Wear personal shielding vests if carried
Keep the active dosimeter running and log the dose
data.escalate: Immediately. Commander decides shelter time with space-weather forecasters.
data.comms_note: The most intense particles can arrive within tens of minutes of a flare, faster than a Mars-to-Earth message.

records.title: Decompression sickness after EVA
records.summary: Joint pain, skin changes, numbness or confusion after a spacewalk.

data.trigger: Joint pain, skin changes, numbness or confusion after a spacewalk.
steps: Report symptoms immediately; do not ignore joint pain
Give 100% oxygen
Re-pressurise the suit or airlock if the protocol says so
Watch for neurological symptoms
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: Pre-breathe protocols before EVA prevent most cases.

records.title: Toxic release (e.g. ammonia leak)
records.summary: Ammonia smell, alarm or visible leak; eye or throat irritation.

data.trigger: Ammonia smell, alarm or visible leak; eye or throat irritation.
steps: Put on emergency masks
Isolate the affected module and close hatches
Flush eyes and skin with water
Move to a safe module
Monitor breathing and SpO₂
data.escalate: Immediately; vehicle emergency procedures run in parallel.
data.comms_note: Ammonia from external cooling loops is one of the ISS's main toxic hazards.

records.title: Fire or smoke exposure
records.summary: Smoke alarm, visible smoke or burning smell.

data.trigger: Smoke alarm, visible smoke or burning smell.
steps: Masks on; follow the vehicle fire checklist
Check each crew member for breathing difficulty
Measure SpO₂; carbon monoxide can make oximeter readings falsely normal
Give oxygen
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: Flames in microgravity are spherical and slow-spreading but hard to locate.

records.title: Foreign body in the eye
records.summary: Eye pain, scratchy feeling, watering after floating debris.

data.trigger: Eye pain, scratchy feeling, watering after floating debris.
steps: Do not rub
Flush with water or saline
Numb with tetracaine drops for inspection only
Stain with fluorescein and photograph under blue light
Send images to the flight surgeon
data.escalate: Same day if pain continues, vision drops or something is embedded.
data.comms_note: One of the most common ISS medical events.

records.title: New vision change (possible SANS)
records.summary: Blurred near vision, distortion on the Amsler grid or a new blind spot.

data.trigger: Blurred near vision, distortion on the Amsler grid or a new blind spot.
steps: Repeat the near-vision card and Amsler grid in each eye
Switch to adjustable-focus glasses
Schedule an onboard eye ultrasound or OCT scan
Log headaches and CO₂ levels
data.escalate: Same day if sudden loss of vision; otherwise next medical conference.
data.comms_note: Gradual near-vision changes are common on long flights.

records.title: Suspected kidney stone
records.summary: Severe flank pain that comes in waves, blood in urine, nausea.

data.trigger: Severe flank pain that comes in waves, blood in urine, nausea.
steps: Give pain relief per protocol
Increase fluids
Use the onboard ultrasound if trained
Strain urine to catch the stone
Watch for fever: a stone with infection is an emergency
data.escalate: Same day; immediately if fever, vomiting or no urine output.
data.comms_note: Bone loss releases calcium into urine, raising risk. Prevention: fluids and potassium citrate.

records.title: Urinary retention
records.summary: Unable to empty the bladder, especially in the first days of flight.

data.trigger: Unable to empty the bladder, especially in the first days of flight.
steps: Try relaxation, privacy and time
Avoid antihistamines and other drugs that worsen retention
Catheterise per protocol if needed
Watch for infection afterwards
data.escalate: If unable to pass urine for 8 h.
data.comms_note: The usual sensation of a full bladder relies partly on gravity.

records.title: Space motion sickness
records.summary: Nausea, vomiting, headache, low appetite in the first 2-3 days in weightlessness or after a gravity change.

data.trigger: Nausea, vomiting, headache, low appetite in the first 2-3 days in weightlessness or after a gravity change.
steps: Limit head movements; keep a consistent visual 'up'
Small, frequent sips of fluid
Antiemetic per protocol
Do not schedule critical tasks during the first dose
data.escalate: If vomiting continues beyond 3 days or fluids cannot be kept down.
data.comms_note: Most crew adapt within a few days.

records.title: Space back pain
records.summary: Low-back ache in the first days or weeks of flight.

data.trigger: Low-back ache in the first days or weeks of flight.
steps: Fetal-position stretches
Pain relief per protocol
Restrain in a curled position for sleep
Report any numbness or weakness
data.escalate: Immediately with leg weakness or loss of bladder control.
data.comms_note: The spine lengthens up to several centimetres without gravity; disc herniation risk rises after return.

records.title: Ongoing sleep loss
records.summary: Under 6 h of sleep for 3 nights or more.

data.trigger: Under 6 h of sleep for 3 nights or more.
steps: Protect a fixed sleep window
Use circadian lighting settings
Reduce noise; earplugs and eye mask
Review workload with the commander
Sleep medication only per protocol
data.escalate: Next private medical conference.
data.comms_note: Station crews average about 6 h of sleep, below the 7 h target.

records.title: Behavioural health crisis
records.summary: Hopelessness, thoughts of self-harm, severe agitation, confusion or a sudden change in behaviour.

data.trigger: Hopelessness, thoughts of self-harm, severe agitation, confusion or a sudden change in behaviour.
steps: Do not leave the person alone
Stay calm; listen; reduce stimulation
Remove access to dangerous items
Contact ground psychiatric support at the first opportunity
Medication only per protocol
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: Isolation and confinement make early, honest check-ins important.

records.title: Severe allergic reaction
records.summary: Hives with breathing difficulty, swelling of lips or throat, or falling blood pressure.

data.trigger: Hives with breathing difficulty, swelling of lips or throat, or falling blood pressure.
steps: Epinephrine auto-injector into the thigh immediately
Oxygen
Antihistamine, then steroid
Second epinephrine dose after 5-15 min if not improving
Monitor for a second reaction over several hours
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: There is no emergency room to go to: treat early.

records.title: Cut or wound
records.summary: Bleeding wound.

data.trigger: Bleeding wound.
steps: Firm pressure until bleeding stops
Clean with saline; capture debris and blood with a towel or suction
Close with strips, glue or stitches with local anaesthetic
Cover and watch for infection
data.escalate: If bleeding does not stop, or for deep or contaminated wounds.
data.comms_note: Blood and fluid form floating droplets: contain them.

records.title: Burn
records.summary: Burn from hot surfaces, electrical faults or chemicals.

data.trigger: Burn from hot surfaces, electrical faults or chemicals.
steps: Cool with water for at least 10 minutes
Remove jewellery and tight items
Cover with a clean, non-stick dressing
Pain relief
data.escalate: Same day for burns larger than the palm, or on face, hands or joints.

records.title: Dental pain or broken tooth
records.summary: Toothache, broken filling or swelling.

data.trigger: Toothache, broken filling or swelling.
steps: Rinse and inspect
Temporary filling material
Pain relief
Antibiotic if signs of infection
data.escalate: If facial swelling or fever.
data.comms_note: Pre-flight dental care is strict because dental problems are hard to treat in space.

records.title: Lunar or Mars dust exposure
records.summary: Coughing, eye irritation or sneezing after EVA or suit doffing.

data.trigger: Coughing, eye irritation or sneezing after EVA or suit doffing.
steps: Vacuum suits before entering the habitat
Flush eyes; use artificial tears
Check SpO₂ and listen for wheezing
Log exposure and symptoms
data.escalate: If breathing difficulty or persistent cough.
data.comms_note: Apollo astronauts reported 'lunar hay fever'. Lunar dust is sharp and abrasive.

records.title: Return to gravity (landing day)
records.summary: After landing on Earth, or arriving on the Moon or Mars after a long transit.

data.trigger: After landing on Earth, or arriving on the Moon or Mars after a long transit.
steps: Fluid and salt loading before entry
Compression garments on
Move the head slowly; sit before standing
Assistance for the first walk
Check blood pressure lying and standing
data.escalate: If fainting or persistent dizziness.
data.comms_note: Balance and blood pressure take days to weeks to fully readapt.

records.title: Deciding without Earth (comms delay)
records.summary: Any serious medical event when the ground reply will take longer than the decision can wait.

data.trigger: Any serious medical event when the ground reply will take longer than the decision can wait.
steps: Crew medical officer leads; commander makes final call
Follow the onboard protocol rather than waiting for a reply
Send a full data package with each step taken
Act on the most recent ground guidance, noting what it was based on
data.escalate: Always inform the ground, even when acting first.
data.comms_note: One-way delay to Mars is 3-22 minutes; there are also periods with no contact.

records.title: Medical evacuation decision
records.summary: A condition that cannot be managed with onboard resources.

data.trigger: A condition that cannot be managed with onboard resources.
steps: Stabilise first
Prepare the vehicle and crew for return if it is possible
Package all medical data for the receiving team
data.escalate: Commander and ground jointly.
data.comms_note: From the ISS, return takes hours. From the Moon, about 3 days. From Mars, there may be no option for months.

records.title: Seizure
records.summary: Sudden jerking, stiffening or loss of awareness.

data.trigger: Sudden jerking, stiffening or loss of awareness.
steps: Keep the person loosely restrained so they cannot strike equipment
Do not put anything in the mouth
Time the seizure
Give a rescue benzodiazepine if it lasts over 5 minutes
Afterwards place them on their side, check SpO₂ and blood sugar
data.escalate: Immediately; any first seizure needs ground review.
data.comms_note: Floating debris and fluids are a choking risk afterwards; keep suction ready.

records.title: Stroke warning signs
records.summary: Face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech or sudden vision loss.

data.trigger: Face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech or sudden vision loss.
steps: Note the exact time symptoms started
Check blood sugar to rule out hypoglycemia
Measure blood pressure and SpO₂
Give oxygen if SpO₂ is below 94%
Do not give aspirin until bleeding has been ruled out by the flight surgeon
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: Treatment options without imaging are very limited; time of onset is the key data point.

records.title: Head injury
records.summary: Struck head on structure or hatch, with headache, confusion or vomiting.

data.trigger: Struck head on structure or hatch, with headache, confusion or vomiting.
steps: Check responsiveness and memory of events
Check pupils and vision with the near-vision card
Pain relief with acetaminophen, not NSAIDs
Neuro checks every hour for 24 hours
No EVA or critical tasks for 24 hours
data.escalate: Immediately with loss of consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting or confusion.
data.comms_note: In microgravity, crew often hit their heads moving through hatches.

records.title: Severe bleeding
records.summary: Bleeding that soaks through dressings or spurts.

data.trigger: Bleeding that soaks through dressings or spurts.
steps: Firm direct pressure with gauze
Pack the wound if deep
Tourniquet above the wound on a limb if pressure fails
Contain floating blood with towels
Check heart rate and blood pressure every 5 minutes
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: Blood forms droplets that float into the cabin and equipment; contain it.

records.title: Suspected fracture
records.summary: Pain, swelling or deformity after impact, especially in wrist, hand or foot.

data.trigger: Pain, swelling or deformity after impact, especially in wrist, hand or foot.
steps: Immobilise with a splint in the position found
Check pulse and feeling beyond the injury
Pain relief
Use ultrasound if trained to look for a break
Elevate and cool
data.escalate: Same day; immediately if pulse or feeling is lost below the injury.
data.comms_note: Bone loss in long missions raises fracture risk, especially after landing.

records.title: Shoulder dislocation
records.summary: Severe shoulder pain with a squared-off shape after a twist or pull.

data.trigger: Severe shoulder pain with a squared-off shape after a twist or pull.
steps: Do not force it back unless trained
Support the arm in the position of comfort
Pain relief
Check pulse and feeling in the hand
Trained crew may reduce it per the checklist
data.escalate: Same day.
data.comms_note: Large forces during EVA or cargo handling can cause it.

records.title: Sprain or strain
records.summary: Pain after twisting a joint or overloading a muscle during exercise.

data.trigger: Pain after twisting a joint or overloading a muscle during exercise.
steps: Rest the area; adjust exercise
Cold pack
Compression wrap
Topical or oral pain relief
data.escalate: If unable to use the joint or no improvement in 3 days.
data.comms_note: Resistive exercise devices apply heavy loads; check form and settings.

records.title: Severe abdominal pain
records.summary: Abdominal pain that is constant, worsening or with fever.

data.trigger: Abdominal pain that is constant, worsening or with fever.
steps: Note where it started and where it is now
Check temperature, heart rate and blood pressure
Nothing by mouth until assessed
Ultrasound if trained
Watch for rebound tenderness or a rigid abdomen
data.escalate: Same day; immediately with fever, rigid abdomen or vomiting blood.
data.comms_note: Appendicitis cannot be operated on in flight; antibiotics may be the only option.

records.title: Vomiting blood or black stool
records.summary: Blood in vomit, coffee-ground vomit, or black tarry stool.

data.trigger: Blood in vomit, coffee-ground vomit, or black tarry stool.
steps: Stop NSAIDs and aspirin
Measure heart rate and blood pressure
Start IV fluids if pulse is fast or BP is low
Acid suppression per protocol
data.escalate: Immediately.

records.title: Severe vomiting or dehydration
records.summary: Unable to keep fluids down, very dark urine or dizziness.

data.trigger: Unable to keep fluids down, very dark urine or dizziness.
steps: Small frequent sips of oral rehydration solution
Antiemetic per protocol
Measure heart rate and blood pressure
IV fluids if oral intake fails
data.escalate: Same day if no urine for 8 hours or fluids cannot be kept down.
data.comms_note: Thirst is blunted in microgravity, so dehydration is easy to miss.

records.title: Diarrhea
records.summary: Three or more loose stools in a day.

data.trigger: Three or more loose stools in a day.
steps: Increase fluids and oral rehydration
Wash hands and clean the hygiene area thoroughly
Antidiarrheal if no fever or blood
Track whether other crew are affected
data.escalate: Same day with fever, blood or more than one crew member affected.
data.comms_note: A gut infection can spread through a small crew quickly.

records.title: Constipation
records.summary: No bowel movement for 3 days or more, or straining.

data.trigger: No bowel movement for 3 days or more, or straining.
steps: Increase fluids and fibre
Increase exercise
Stool softener, then osmotic laxative if needed
data.escalate: If severe abdominal pain or vomiting.
data.comms_note: Low fluids, low fibre and opioids all contribute.

records.title: Urinary tract infection
records.summary: Burning on urination, frequency, cloudy urine.

data.trigger: Burning on urination, frequency, cloudy urine.
steps: Increase fluids
Check temperature
Urine test strip if available
Antibiotic per protocol
data.escalate: Same day with fever, flank pain or vomiting (possible kidney infection).
data.comms_note: Incomplete bladder emptying raises infection risk.

records.title: Ear pain or blocked ears
records.summary: Ear pain, fullness or muffled hearing, often after pressure changes.

data.trigger: Ear pain, fullness or muffled hearing, often after pressure changes.
steps: Swallow, yawn or gently equalise
Decongestant spray before pressure changes
Check for discharge or fever
Ear drops if infection is suspected
data.escalate: If severe pain, discharge or hearing loss.
data.comms_note: Cabin pressure changes before EVA or vehicle docking can trigger it.

records.title: Nosebleed
records.summary: Bleeding from the nose.

data.trigger: Bleeding from the nose.
steps: Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes
Capture blood with gauze; it will not drip away
Decongestant spray on gauze if it continues
Check blood pressure
data.escalate: If it lasts over 30 minutes or follows a head injury.
data.comms_note: Dry cabin air and headward fluid shift make nosebleeds more likely.

records.title: Chemical in the eye
records.summary: Splash of chemical, cleaning agent or coolant into the eye.

data.trigger: Splash of chemical, cleaning agent or coolant into the eye.
steps: Flush immediately with water or saline for at least 15 minutes
Hold the eyelids open
Identify the chemical from the label
Check vision afterwards and photograph the eye
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: Liquids do not run off in microgravity; flushing needs a contained setup.

records.title: Skin infection or abscess
records.summary: Red, hot, swollen, painful skin, possibly with pus.

data.trigger: Red, hot, swollen, painful skin, possibly with pus.
steps: Mark the edge of the redness with a pen
Warm compresses
Antibiotic per protocol
Drain an abscess only if trained
data.escalate: Same day if redness spreads past the mark or fever develops.
data.comms_note: Slower healing and immune changes make infections more likely.

records.title: Allergic or contact rash
records.summary: Itchy red rash after contact with a new material or product.

data.trigger: Itchy red rash after contact with a new material or product.
steps: Remove the suspected cause
Wash the area
Hydrocortisone cream
Oral antihistamine for itch
data.escalate: Immediately if lips, tongue or breathing are affected.
data.comms_note: New materials arriving on cargo vehicles can trigger reactions.

records.title: Shingles (viral reactivation)
records.summary: Painful band of blisters on one side of the body.

data.trigger: Painful band of blisters on one side of the body.
steps: Start antiviral early
Pain relief
Cover the rash; wash hands
Check eyes if the rash is on the face
data.escalate: Same day; immediately if near the eye.
data.comms_note: Latent viruses reactivate more often in spaceflight.

records.title: Cold exposure
records.summary: Shivering, confusion or clumsiness after EVA or a cooling fault.

data.trigger: Shivering, confusion or clumsiness after EVA or a cooling fault.
steps: Move to a warm module
Remove damp clothing; insulate
Warm drinks if fully alert
Measure core temperature
data.escalate: Immediately if confused or temperature is below 35 °C.
data.comms_note: Spacesuit cooling and heating faults can cause rapid temperature changes.

records.title: Heat stress
records.summary: Hot, flushed, headache, fast pulse, during exercise or a suit cooling failure.

data.trigger: Hot, flushed, headache, fast pulse, during exercise or a suit cooling failure.
steps: Stop activity; remove heat source
Increase airflow with fans
Cool with damp cloths
Fluids if alert
Check temperature every 15 minutes
data.escalate: Immediately if temperature is above 39 °C or confused.
data.comms_note: Without convection, body heat escapes more slowly in microgravity.

records.title: Electrical shock
records.summary: Contact with a live circuit.

data.trigger: Contact with a live circuit.
steps: Isolate the power before touching the person
Check breathing and pulse
Attach the defibrillator if unresponsive
Look for entry and exit burns
ECG monitoring for arrhythmias
data.escalate: Immediately.

records.title: Choking
records.summary: Unable to speak, cough or breathe after eating.

data.trigger: Unable to speak, cough or breathe after eating.
steps: Ask: are you choking?
Brace both of you against a wall or restraint
Give abdominal thrusts; in microgravity the rescuer must be anchored
If unresponsive, start CPR and look in the mouth for the object
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: Floating food crumbs make inhaled debris a real hazard.

records.title: Asthma attack or bronchospasm
records.summary: Wheezing, tight chest, difficulty breathing out.

data.trigger: Wheezing, tight chest, difficulty breathing out.
steps: Sit upright, calm breathing
Reliever inhaler with spacer
Check SpO₂
Add ipratropium and a steroid if not improving
Oxygen if SpO₂ is below 94%
data.escalate: Immediately if unable to speak in full sentences or SpO₂ is below 92%.
data.comms_note: Dust, smoke and cabin chemicals can trigger it.

records.title: Suspected collapsed lung
records.summary: Sudden sharp chest pain on one side with breathlessness.

data.trigger: Sudden sharp chest pain on one side with breathlessness.
steps: Oxygen
Check SpO₂ and heart rate
Ultrasound if trained (lung sliding)
Prepare for needle decompression by trained crew if worsening
data.escalate: Immediately.
data.comms_note: Pressure changes during EVA preparation are a possible trigger.

records.title: Palpitations or irregular heartbeat
records.summary: Racing, pounding or irregular heartbeat.

data.trigger: Racing, pounding or irregular heartbeat.
steps: Sit quietly and record heart rate
Record an ECG if available
Try vagal manoeuvres (bear down) for a fast regular rhythm
Check for caffeine, decongestants or dehydration
data.escalate: Immediately with chest pain, fainting or breathlessness.
data.comms_note: Cardiac rhythm changes have been recorded in some long-duration crew.

records.title: High blood pressure
records.summary: Blood pressure 160/100 or higher on two readings.

data.trigger: Blood pressure 160/100 or higher on two readings.
steps: Repeat after 15 minutes of seated rest
Review decongestants, salt and sleep
Check for headache, vision change or chest pain
data.escalate: Same day if it stays high; immediately with symptoms.
